rules.title: Word formation
rules.rule: -aro makes the doer (legaro "soldier", alkimiaro "alchemist"); -ato/-ito the thing done (jubato "decree"); -anza an abstract noun (telanza "valour"); -ino something small (kaimino "cottage"); -orio a workplace (ardorio "furnace"); -ia a land or domain (Keria); -aire a house or domain (Vaire, Exaire); -s dignity (Luxis, Keras). Verbs come from nouns with -are (kera "crown" > kerare "to crown"). Compounds put the head first (reino + Vaire = Reinovaire).

rules.title: Personal and house names
rules.rule: A person has a given name and a house name, in that order (Rechtar Vaire, Doir Vaire, Rundir Voidet). The house name is the "owner" in head-first order: Rechtar "of" Vaire. Given names are not marked for sex (Rechtar, Doir). Great houses end in -aire "house, domain" (Vaire); lesser families often take a descriptive name (Voidet "of the emptiness").

rules.title: Titles
rules.rule: Titles come before the name: Keraro Rechtar Vaire "Emperor Rechtar Vaire". keraro "crown-bearer" is the Emperor at court; soldiers say imperaru "commander" (KED-REG-04). primaro "first priest" is the head of the Domo Luxis, the Church of Light (Rechtar took the title in 0 a.v.e.; English lore calls it Pope). reiato "regent, governor" is Doir Vaire's title over the Vilnayan towns. sedaro is a judge, duko a general, alkimiaro supraro the head of the Imperial Academy of Alchemy.

rules.title: Place names
rules.rule: Domains end in -aire (Reinovaire, Exaire "domain of the springs", Arbaire "domain of the trees"); lands in -ia (Keria); holy cities and gods take dignity -s, which gives the endings -as and -is (Keras "the Crowned", Luxis). Kedre calls the empire's homeland Valnor, a Norsund word ("north Valia") borrowed back.

rules.title: Court decree
rules.rule: Decrees begin with the verb and name the ruler in the third person (Juba Rechtar Vaire ...), list the commands as short clauses joined by ed, and close with the place and year (Aro nulo, Keras).

rules.title: Church liturgy
rules.rule: Prayers address the goddess by her dignity name in the vocative position at the start of the line (Luxis, ...), use the subjunctive for every wish, and close with "Sik sia" ("so be it").

rules.title: The Academy's learned style
rules.rule: Writers of the Imperial Academy of Alchemy pile up participle nouns and numbers, prefer the passive (es mixtato "is mixed"), and coin terms with -anza and -orio. Norsund's learned loans (alkimia, medikina, kupola) come from this style.

rules.title: Camp Kedre (soldiers and traders)
rules.rule: The speech of the legions and camp-followers in Thiolden kept an older final -u where court Kedre has -o (camp kividu, imperaru, denaru, molu, obsidiu, probu, pagu, sodalu, kastellu beside court kivido, imperaro, denaro, molo, obsidio, probo, pago, sodalo, kastello), clipped titles and swore by the Emperor rather than by Luxis. Norsund heard Kedre mostly in this form, which is why its occupation loans cite camp forms. The u-ending also survives in merkadu everywhere.

rules.title: Dates
rules.rule: Kedre counts years from the founding of the Empire, Keria: aro N post Keria "year N after Keria" (English a.v.e.) and aro N ante Keria "year N before Keria" (b.v.e.). Year zero is aro nulo. Rechtar's conquest of Thiolden began aro trimi dekre ed sevi post Keria (37 a.v.e.).

rules.title: How Kedre words entered Norsund
rules.rule: Occupation-era loans (37-51 a.v.e. and Doir Vaire's rule) lost their final vowel, simplified double consonants and moved stress to the first syllable: murra > mur, merkadu > merk, kampo > kamp, porta > port, turra > tur. In rivia > rie the v between vowels was also lost and the ending was heard as Norsund unstressed -e. Learned loans, taken later from books, kept their shape and stress: alkimia, medikina, kupola. The same word borrowed twice gives a doublet (tur and turra in Norsund). These are the "occupation" and "learned" layers of records/languages/norsund/grammar/12-registers-dialects.yaml (kedre_layers) and its rule REG-02.

rules.title: Camp forms behind the occupation loans
rules.rule: Most occupation loans were heard in camp Kedre (KED-REG-04): kividu > kivid "citizen", imperaru > imperar "emperor", denaru > denar "coin", molu > mol "pier", obsidiu > obsid "siege", probu > prov "test", pagu > pag "pay", sodalu > sodal "guild", kastellu > kastell "fortress". The cognate pairs (telo/thiol, fovo/dov) are not loans: they come down from Proto-Valian through the pv-kedre and Norsund stages of 13-history.

rules.title: Norsund words in Kedre
rules.rule: Kedre borrowed runa from Norsund run to name the rune magic of Thiolden (native runo means only "secret"), and Valnor for its own homeland. Rundir Voidet's rune explosives are krepito runa, "rune powder".

context: Old Norsund is the language of the settlers who came to Thiolden from the island of Farheim around 450 b.v.e. It gave way to Norsund around 100 a.v.e.
It survives as the high register for oaths, law, temple liturgy, rune-craft and sagas (records/languages/norsund/grammar/12-registers-dialects.yaml).
Its word forms are the output of the pv-pn and pn-on stages in records/languages/norsund/grammar/13-history.yaml. The Old Norsund column of the cognate table there is authoritative.
Glosses follow the Leipzig Glossing Rules. NOM nominative, ACC accusative, GEN genitive, DAT dative, AN animate, IN inanimate, OPT optative, AGT agent.

after_vowel.note: A stem ending in -i drops the i before an ending that begins with a vowel: negi, ACC nega, GEN negis, DAT nege, PL negin.

article.position: after the noun, as a separate word

adjectives.agreement: Adjectives take the case and number endings of the noun's class (thiola Vilkyra 'brave free sword' ACC).

relative.note: invariable; replaced by the Kedre loan ke in Norsund

verbs.strong_verbs: Same ablaut classes as Norsund (lida leid lidin, dola dul dolin, vetha vath vothin, aga og agin ...); the participle ends in -in.

irregular.gloss: to owe, to be bound to (future auxiliary)
to be able, to have the power to

numbers.tens: unit + dovthamm as two words: 20 dov dovthamm, 70 sev dovthamm (Norsund dovtamm, sevtamm)

correlatives.note: Old Norsund wrote the indefinite, negative and universal forms as two words; Norsund fused them (yn kum > ynkum).

rules.title: Sounds
rules.rule: Old Norsund has the same consonants and vowels as Norsund, with three differences. g between vowels is still a stop (negi, later nay). Words may begin with hw (hwander, later wander). The diphthong ey (from umlaut of au) has not yet merged with ei. Long vowels exist and are written double in ASCII (tiir "glory").

rules.title: Full vowels in endings
rules.rule: Unstressed endings keep their full vowels: animate plural -in, present -ur, strong participle -in. The Norsund reduction rule later turned them into -en, -er, -en, all pronounced [ən]/[ər].

rules.title: Stress
rules.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable of every word, as in Norsund. There are no Kedre loans in true Old Norsund.

rules.title: Two ways to write it
rules.rule: In English-language lore, write Old Norsund in the plain ASCII romanization used for Norsund (th, kj, double vowels for length). Scholarly citations may use þ for th at the start of a word, ð for th between vowels and at the end of a word after a vowel, and an acute accent for long vowels: thiol = þjol, vetha = veða, tiir = tír. Reconstructed Proto-Norsund forms are starred (*kjoldu).

rules.title: Four cases
rules.rule: Nouns have four cases: nominative (subject), accusative (object), genitive (possession) and dative (after prepositions and for the receiver of a gift). Animate nouns mark the accusative singular with -a; inanimate nouns use the same form for nominative and accusative, like neuter nouns in older Germanic languages. All prepositions take the dative.

rules.title: Noun paradigms
rules.rule: Animate and inanimate nouns differ in the accusative singular and in the plural.

rules.title: The article was still a word
rules.rule: Old Norsund had no suffixed article. "The" was the word hin (plural hine) placed after the noun: kyr hin "the blade". In Norsund it fused onto the noun as -in, -ene and -arne. It fused after the reduction rule had stopped, which is why the singular -in kept its i while the old plural -in became -en.

rules.title: Genitives may follow
rules.rule: In law and verse a genitive often follows its noun (lag Kjoldmuri "the law of the Kjoldmur"). In ordinary speech it came first, as it does in Norsund (Tyri kyr).

rules.title: Adjectives agree
rules.rule: Adjectives stand before the noun and take its case and number endings. Norsund lost this agreement.

rules.title: Pronouns and possessives
rules.rule: Personal pronouns have four cases (table above). The plural pronouns end in -in, which became -en in Norsund (emin > emen, selin > selen). Possessive pronouns (the genitive forms) follow the noun: kyr emi "my blade".

rules.title: Verbs agree in number
rules.rule: The present and past still distinguish a singular and a plural subject: kjoldur "guards" (one), kjoldum "guard" (several). Norsund kept only the singular form for every subject.

rules.title: Optative instead of ma
rules.rule: Wishes, blessings and curses use the optative ending -i (plural -im). Blessings usually put the subject first (Myr kjoldi heim "may Myr guard the home"); curses put the verb first (Biti kyr emi om "may my blade bite me"). Norsund replaced the optative with ma + infinitive; ma is worn down from maga "to have the power to".

rules.title: Future with hala
rules.rule: hala "to owe, to be bound to" + infinitive expresses what will or must happen. Its present halur wore down to the Norsund future auxiliary hal; its past halde became Norsund halde "would".

examples.form: Kjold eth grith hal-ur mur ves-a.
examples.gloss: ward and sanctuary owe-PRS.SG wall be-INF
examples.translation: Ward and sanctuary the wall shall be.

rules.title: Verb second, verb last
rules.rule: Main clauses are verb-second, as in Norsund. Subordinate clauses put the finite verb last, with ne right before it (sof em vath brestur "if I break the oath"). Norsund later moved the verb forward to subject-verb-object in all clauses.

examples.translation: whoever does not guard the wall

rules.title: Negation
rules.rule: ne comes directly before the finite verb in every clause (Em ne skrinkur "I do not flee"). In Norsund main clauses it moved after the verb.

rules.title: Relative clauses
rules.rule: The invariable particle ys introduces relative clauses. Norsund replaced it with the Kedre loan ke.

rules.title: No evidentials
rules.rule: Old Norsund has no evidential particles. Oaths name the gods as witnesses instead (Sajir es Myr "Myr is witness"). To modern ears the old oaths sound strangely bare, which is part of their solemnity.

rules.title: Where Old Norsund is still heard
rules.rule: Vilkyr oaths, the laws carved on the Kjoldmur, the oldest temple invocations (which use the old god-names Myr and Heid), sagas, and every rune-craft formula. Farheim island speech keeps some Old Norsund forms in everyday songs.

rules.title: Syllables and clusters
rules.rule: Old Norsund syllables follow the Norsund onset and coda lists (records/languages/norsund/grammar/01-phonology.yaml), with two additions: hw- may begin a word (hwander), and a vowel may end a word after k or g (negi, because the final-i-loss rule of 13-history spared velars). Endings keep full vowels, so words often have one more clear syllable than their Norsund descendants.

rules.title: Reading runes
rules.rule: The rune-row (records/languages/scripts/runar.yaml) writes one rune per sound, but carvers did not mark long vowels or double consonants, and they wrote no vowel twice in a row. A word divider (a dot or two) separates words. Scholars normalize a carving into the plain spelling: the runes for t-i-r may stand for tir or tiir "glory". When a reading is uncertain, give the normalized form and say so.

examples.translation: a carving that may be read kull vas hel 'the ember was good' (kul for kull)

rules.title: Full noun paradigms
rules.rule: Every noun follows one of four patterns: animate, inanimate, vowel stem, or umlaut plural (tables ON-T2 and ON-T3). Prepositions take the dative. The dative plural -um is the same for every class.

rules.title: Umlaut plurals in the cases
rules.rule: The six umlaut nouns (lud/lyd, thamm/themm, gat/get, fuld/fyld, tunn/tynn, brod/bred) change the vowel in every plural case and add the plural case endings to it: lyd, lydi, lydum. The singular is regular animate: lud, luda, ludi, lude.

rules.title: Comparison
rules.rule: Comparative -ar, superlative -ast, then the agreement ending (thiolara Vilkyra "the braver free sword", ACC). Four adjectives are irregular and were inherited unchanged by Norsund: hel batar bast, vond verr verst, myk meir mest, lit minn minst. "Than" is thon, followed by the nominative.

rules.title: Numbers
rules.rule: Old Norsund counts in tens, but ten is still dovthamm "two hands" and tens are two words: dov dovthamm "twenty", sev dovthamm "seventy". Teens add eth "and": dovthamm eth yn "eleven". Norsund contracted these to tamm, dovtamm, tammyn. Markets counted goods in the long hundred, langhaun (120). Numbers above one take a plural noun in the case the sentence needs.

rules.title: Ordinals
rules.rule: Ordinals add -de after voiced sounds and -te after voiceless ones (thrimde, veste); "first" is ura, "from the origin". Ordinals inflect like adjectives. Seven is sev everywhere: the Starisund form stev did not yet exist.

rules.title: Reflexive, reciprocal and demonstratives
rules.rule: sjo "self" serves every person and does not inflect; sjosjo means "each other". The demonstratives hes "this" and thas "that" inflect like adjectives (hesar runar "these runes", thasa ACC). In memorial formulas the demonstrative follows its noun: runar hesar.

rules.title: Question words and their family
rules.rule: The question words are the same as in Norsund (kum, kut, kur, kuna, kuvi, kuso, kumik, kul). The "some-", "no-" and "every-" words are still two words: yn kum "someone", ne kut "nothing", al kur "everywhere". kum and kut inflect like animate and inanimate nouns (kuma "whom", kuti "whose").

rules.title: Weak verb paradigm
rules.rule: Weak verbs agree with a singular or plural subject in the present and past (table ON-T4). The infinitive ends in -a, the imperative is the bare stem, and the optative is -i (singular) or -im (plural).

rules.title: Strong verbs
rules.rule: Strong verbs change their vowel for the past, as in Norsund, and add -um for a plural subject (dul "fell", dulum "they fell"). The participle ends in -in, which Norsund reduced to -en. Principal parts are listed in the morphology block above.

examples.translation: The ships went out from Farheim.

rules.title: Perfect, passive and participles
rules.rule: The perfect is aga "have" + participle (agur kjoldad "has guarded"); the passive is vesa + participle (es vothin "is bound"). The present participle -ande works as an adjective and agrees (lysande run "a shining rune").

rules.title: Coordination and subordination
rules.rule: eth "and", ava "but", vo "or" join clauses without changing word order. Subordinate clauses put the finite verb last: sof "if", kuna "when", ys "that, which, who", ter ys "because", for ys "before", aft ys "after", thon "than". ys is both the relative and the complementizer; Norsund replaced it with ke, so Norsund ter ke continues ter ys.

examples.form: Em ne skrink-ur, ter ys Myr om kjold-ur.
examples.gloss: 1SG.NOM NEG flee-PRS.SG because REL Myr 1SG.ACC guard-PRS.SG
examples.translation: I do not flee, because Myr guards me.

rules.title: Word formation
rules.rule: Old Norsund builds words as Norsund does: compounds with the head last (nimkjold), the linking genitive -i- (starisund), and the suffixes -ir (agent: skilir "judge"), -ning (deed or result), -eth (quality: thioleth), -ling (small or young), -ug (full of), -nuth (without), -a (adjectives and verbs), and the prefixes ne-, mar-, ur-, al-. Several of these suffixes now look the same in both languages, but not by inheritance. The reduction rule turned inherited -ir into -er (Old kjoldir became Norsund kjolder). Norsund then re-borrowed -ir, -ning, -ling and -ug from Old Norsund law and liturgy in their old shape, as English borrowed learned Latin endings.

rules.title: Kennings
rules.rule: Kennings came from Old Norsund verse and are still composed in it. The base noun takes the case of the sentence; the modifier stays in the genitive or is compounded. Kennings may nest.

rules.title: Personal names and bynames
rules.rule: A person is named by given name + parent-name in -ung ("child of"; Alkregg > Alkreggung) and, for the famous, a byname: adjective or noun + the article hin after it (Tyr thiol hin, "Tyr the brave"). In Norsund the article fused and the byname became Tyr Thiolin. Given names are one or two name elements (Aur + hask = Aurhask "silver-axe"). Inherited Farheim names (Astrid, Haakon, Ulf) are older than Old Norsund itself.

rules.title: Houses and memorial stones
rules.rule: A house is "the children of" its founder: founder + -ungin (Norsund -ungen). Memorial stones follow a fixed formula: WHO carved these runes after WHOM (dative), relationship; a line of praise; a blessing in the optative; and a closing ban on charging the runes, because rune magic near the dead raises them.

examples.translation: carved these runes in memory of Aurhask

rules.title: The oath register
rules.rule: Oaths are first person, present tense, and end with the gods named as witnesses (Sajir es Myr) and a conditional curse in the optative (Sof em vath brestur, biti kyr emi om). The hand on the blade (a kyre eth a thamme) is part of the formula.

rules.title: The law register
rules.rule: Laws open with Hes es lag X-i ("this is the law of X"). Each rule is a relative clause plus a main clause: Kum ys ... , thas ... ("whoever ..., that one ..."). Penalties use the future auxiliary hala or the noun utlag. Judgments close with Sva skilum emin. A witness who did not see may not swear. That is the root of the Auristar rule that testimony without the evidential sa is hearsay.

rules.title: The liturgy register
rules.rule: Invocations open with Em heitur X-a ("I call upon X"), use the old god-names Myr and Heid, make requests with the imperative jov "give" or the optative, and close with Sva es urlag ("so is fate"). Modern Starisund priests add stari after these lines.

rules.title: The saga register
rules.rule: Sagas open with Hes es frast X-i ("this is the tale of X") and tell events in the past tense, with short clauses joined by eth and ava. Time is counted in days and nights (a nyvde dage "on the ninth day"). Speech is quoted with mal "said".

rules.title: Rune-magic incantations
rules.rule: An incantation has a fixed shape: the carver names the act (Run ristur em, run ladur em, "a rune I carve, a rune I charge"), names the powers (vald, the arcane field; sveim, the aether current), commands the runes in the optative, and ends with Glod! ("glow!"). Then the runes glow. Charging runes is rune magic: it destroyed Marheim, it is forbidden in Auristar by the law of the Kjoldmur, and a glowing rune in Auristar is always a crime or a sign of forbidden magic. Plain runic writing never glows.

rules.title: Old Norsund verse
rules.rule: Old Norsund verse uses the sundlag of records/languages/norsund/grammar/14-poetics.yaml: two half-lines of two stresses, linked by alliteration on the first stressed syllable of the second half. The full endings give more unstressed syllables than Norsund, so the old lines sound longer and heavier. Heiti (jor, bran, ljom, varg, log, berg, dreyr) replace everyday nouns.

examples.form: Skryma thiarkur em · em ne skrinkur
examples.translation: The monster I hunt · I shrink not (sk alliterates)

rules.title: Where Old Norsund came from
rules.rule: Old Norsund is Proto-Valian after the pv-pn and pn-on stages of 13-history. Grimm-style shifts (grimm-1, grimm-2, grimm-3) gave its consonants. Breaking (breaking-u) gave thiol from *telu and kjold from *geldhu. Palatalization gave kj; umlaut gave kyr from *guri and myr from *muri. final-u-loss and final-i-loss shortened words like *staru to star; ln-assimilation gave kull. The Old Norsund column of the 31 cognate sets is authoritative.

rules.title: How Old Norsund became Norsund
rules.rule: Sound changes of the on-n stage of 13-history: ey-merger (ey > ei); g-gliding and glide-i-loss with ej-diphthong (negi > nay); reduction (final -in, -ur > -en, -er: Vilkyrin > Vilkyren, kjoldur > kjolder); unstressed-shortening (iliin > ilin); hw-simplification (hwander > wander). Grammar changes: the cases fell away except the genitive; number agreement on verbs and adjectives was lost; the article hin fused onto the noun as -in after reduction had stopped; subordinate clauses became subject-verb-object; ne moved after the verb in main clauses; the Kedre loan ke replaced ys; ma (from maga) replaced the optative; hal (from halur) became the future auxiliary. Evidentials grew out of Old words: sa is the past of saja, sund is the noun "song", and stari is the genitive of star.

scripts.name: Lysrit
scripts.type: featural alphabet written in syllable cells
scripts.direction: left to right, cells on one line
context: Auristar's sacred and civic script, designed by Starlight Library scholars (c. 99-124 a.v.e.). It is systematic because it was designed, as Hangul was.
Used for temples, the Kjoldmur, decrees of the Seven Lights, holy names and civic monuments. Everyday writing in Auristar still uses runes, which never glow there.
tools/norsund/scripts.js renders Lysrit to SVG from these tables; assets/fonts/Lysrit-Regular.otf types it from the romanization.
The glyphs of the v0.1 proposal (2026-11-19) are kept unchanged.

grid.nodes: C is the centre; nodes 0-6 sit on the rim at angle -90 + k*360/7 degrees, clockwise from the top point (node 0).
grid.same_as_emblem: The seven rim nodes are the points of Auristar's emblem, top point up.
grid.grid_nodes: Every cell shows the eight grid nodes as faint dots (radius 1.15). In carving they may be drilled or set with crystal; in small type they may be left out.

vowels.note: high front rounded; the top point
the unstressed e of final syllables (-en, -er, -ade). The romanization writes e; Lysrit writes the difference.

marks.name: voiced
marks.form: lit centre: filled star-coloured dot, radius 2.7

marks.name: long vowel
marks.form: ring of radius 6.2 around the vowel star

marks.name: geminate
marks.form: short bar under the cell, from x 14 to 26 at y 41.5

marks.name: number
marks.form: bar over the cell, the full cell width at y 2.6, so adjacent number cells join into one bar

marks.name: sacred
marks.form: violet seven-pointed star (heptagram, outer radius 9, inner 3.8) in a 26-unit cell before a holy word

cells: A cell holds at most one consonant and the vowel stars that follow it (at most two).
A vowel with no consonant before it, or a third vowel, opens an empty cell of its own.
A doubled consonant is one geminate cell; a doubled vowel is one long star.
th, kj, gj and ng are single consonants. ei, ay, au and ou are two stars in one cell.
c, q, x and z are not Norsund letters. When a foreign name must be written they become k, k, ks and s.
An unstressed e in the last syllable of a word of two or more syllables is drawn as ə (node 4).
Words are separated by a gap of 14 units, or by the word divider in inscriptions.

numerals.system: 1 to 7 trace the rim clockwise from the top point, one edge per unit; 7 is the closed heptagon, the "full count". 8 lights the centre of the closed heptagon; 9 adds the ray from the centre to the top point. 0 is a hollow centre, nuth "the void". The long hundred (langhaun, 120) is the closed heptagon with Auristar's seven-pointed star drawn inside it in fine lines; it is used as a unit sign in old market reckoning (3 + long hundred = 360).

examples.note: one closed heptagon: the Seven Lights, the seven days of the Council games
Auristar's population: six number cells under one bar

punctuation.name: comma
punctuation.form: short vertical stroke low in the cell

punctuation.name: question
punctuation.form: vertical stroke under a small star

evidential_sigils.form: a ring around a star at the centre (an eye)
three stars across the middle: nodes 5, centre, 2
a star on every rim node: the full sky

rules.title: Building a word
rules.rule: Split the word into consonants and vowels, group each consonant with the vowels that follow it, and draw one cell per group: the consonant's strokes, the lit centre if it is voiced, then the vowel stars.

rules.title: Holy names
rules.rule: Gods, the Auristar, the Seven Lights and the Fall of the Star take the violet sacred mark before them.

rules.title: Inscription style
rules.rule: In carved stone the strokes are V-cut, the grid nodes are drilled, and vowel stars and lit centres are set with Starifjolden crystal. Words are separated by the diamond divider instead of a space.

rules.title: Cursive (scribal hand)
rules.rule: Scribes of the Starlight Library write a fast hand in which the grid nodes are left out, stars become plain dots, and the last stroke of each cell runs on into the first stroke of the next along the baseline. The cursive is never used for holy names, which are always written in full cells.

rules.title: Light-writing at night
rules.rule: Because every letter is a pattern of points, Lysrit can be written with lights alone: lit windows or crystal studs at the node positions spell words across a tower face after dark. Stars and lit centres burn brightest; strokes are implied.

design_notes: The script's single physical metaphor is the constellation. Keep strokes straight, stars four-pointed and the grid visible.
Palette: ink in deep navy (#121733) on white stone, stars and lit centres in cyan (#0a7584 on light, #8ef0ff on dark), sacred marks in violet (#8a33a8).
For stained glass, strokes become lead lines, stars become small cyan panes and the lit centre a jewel; the heptagon rim may be leaded as a frame.
For techwear, each cell suits embroidery or laser-cut panels; a word reads well as a vertical strip of cells on a sleeve or strap.
In game UI, keep cells at 24 px or larger; below that, drop the grid nodes.
Lysrit has no circles crossed by lines and no spoked wheels. The only radial figures are Auristar's own seven-pointed star and the heptagon.

scripts.name: The runes (runar)
scripts.direction: left to right; on round stones and staffs the line may turn with the surface
context: The everyday script of Thiolden, inherited from the Old Norsund settlers of Farheim.

Canon (records/user-submitted-stories/marv.yaml) says runes are "just the written word of the people alive at that time". Runes become rune magic only when charged with aether, and a charged rune glows. Auristar forbids rune magic but not rune writing, so runes in Auristar never glow.

These runes are an original design for the Drunken Dragon Universe. Some single shapes coincide with historical runes, but with different sound values; runar are not a cipher of the Elder or Younger Futhark.
tools/norsund/scripts.js renders runes to SVG from these tables; assets/fonts/Runar-Regular.otf (long-branch) and Runar-Twig.otf (short-twig) type them.
design_principles: Consonants carry their strokes on the right of the stave; vowels on the left. No rune has strokes on both sides.

design_principles.Where the sound is made decides the stro: lips use a bow, the tongue tip a falling branch, the back of the mouth a rising branch.

design_principles: How it is made decides the height. Stops use the top, fricatives the middle, nasals the bottom; liquids and glides use two strokes.
A voiced stop or fricative adds the heel at the foot of the stave.
kj and gj are k and g with the palatal dot.
Vowels are single strokes on the left. Front vowels rise (i, e), back vowels fall (o, u), and a and y are bows.
No curves. Every stroke can be cut with a knife across or along the grain.

variants.use: stone, monuments, boundary stones, anything meant to last
wood, bone, tallies, letters and everyday notes
variants.rule: Every stroke is pulled halfway toward the point where it meets the stave (a falling branch from (0, r) ends at (0.25, r + 0.15); a bow keeps its centre and halves its size). Stave, heel position and dots stay where they are.

spelling: One rune per sound. th, kj, gj and ng are single runes.
Long vowels and double consonants are written by repeating the rune (aa, ll).
Diphthongs (ei/ay, au, ou) are two runes. The unstressed e of endings is the e rune.
c and q are written with the k rune, x with k + s, z with s.
Words are separated by a single dot (·) and sentences by two dots (:), as on old runestones.

numerals.system: Runes have no digit signs. Numbers are written as words, or in merchants' tallies: one tally group per decimal digit, most significant first. One to four are short notches; five is a "hand", a long stroke slanted across four notches; six to nine are a hand followed by notches; zero is a short level dash. Vilnayan merchants also count goods in long hundreds (langhaun, 120), cutting a notch on a separate stick for each long hundred.

magic: Writing a rune is not magic. A rune becomes magic only when the carver charges it with aether while cutting it.
A charged rune glows (cyan-white in art). Glow is the only visual sign of rune magic.
Auristar law: runes may be written anywhere in the city, but never charged. In Auristar art and character design, runes never glow.
The rune magic used at Marheim (50 a.v.e.) was a mass charging of runes cut into siege charges; that is why the undead rose there.
Rune names are recited when carving charged runes; a wrongly cut or wrongly named rune is the classic cause of a spell gone wrong.

new_words.note: name of the ng rune; the same element as the parent-name suffix -ung

hate_symbol_screening.status: Screened 2026-11-19 against the listed ADL entries; no rune matches. The rules below are enforced by tools/test/scripts.test.mjs in CI.
avoided: Othala / Odal rune, with or without "wings" or feet (a diamond on two legs)
Algiz / "Life rune" (a stave with a symmetric fork) and the inverted "Death rune"
Sowilo / "Sig rune", single or doubled (lightning-bolt zigzag)
Wolfsangel (a Z or hook with a crossbar)
Hagal (Armanen six-armed rune, a stave crossed by an X)
Black Sun (sunwheel of sig runes), Totenkopf, Celtic cross (cross in a circle), triskele and sunwheels
swastika-like composites and bind-runes of any of the above
how: No rune has strokes on both sides of the stave, so no rune can form a symmetric fork, an arrowhead, an X or a crossed stave.
No rune is a closed diamond, and no rune has a zigzag without a stave.
The t rune is not called "tyr", to avoid the "Tyr rune" association; it is tar "tear, drop".
Bind-runes (two runes sharing one stave) are not part of runar. Logos, sigils and props must not stack runes into composite marks.
Lysrit has no spoked wheels or crossed circles; its only radial figures are Auristar's seven-pointed star and the heptagon.

rules.title: Reading direction
rules.rule: Left to right. Consonants "look forward" (strokes to the right) and vowels "look back" (strokes to the left).

rules.title: Which form to cut
rules.rule: Long-branch for stone and anything permanent, short-twig for wood, bone and quick notes. Both spell the same way.

rules.title: Never glowing in Auristar
rules.rule: Runes on Auristar buildings, armour and clothing are cut, inked, embroidered or inlaid, but never glowing. A glowing rune in Auristar is a crime scene.

context: Version 1.0.0, part of the Norsund language build approved on 2026-11-19. The full grammar (34 rules), dictionary (384 entries) and texts (6 texts) live beside this record.
Dates use the Vairean imperial system (b.v.e. / a.v.e.).
facts: Kedre is the language of the Vairean Empire. Its name means "the Tongue".
Kedre is spoken in Keras, the imperial city, and in the old Kingdom of Reinovaire, in Valnor.
Kedre and Norsund are distant cousins; both descend from Proto-Valian.
Lysmar (Norsund) and Luxis (Kedre) are the same word in the two branches, both meaning light.
Most Kedre words end in a vowel, and stress falls on the second-to-last syllable.
Kedre has no th, y or w sounds, and no kj or gj.
Kedre writes k for the k sound (Keras, Keria), x for ks (Luxis) and j for the y-sound of "yes".
Kedre puts the head of a phrase first (Reinovaire "realm of Vaire", sangia Vaire "the bloodline of Vaire"), the opposite of Norsund.
The suffix -s marks gods, imperial titles and holy cities (Luxis, Keras).
Kedre has no gender, no case and no articles. Plurals change the final vowel (legia, legie).
Verbs fall into two classes, -are and -ire, with person endings, a past in -av-/-iv-, a subjunctive in -ia, a future with vole and a passive with esere.
Imperial decrees begin with the verb; prayers end with "Sik sia", "so be it".
ke introduces every subordinate clause.
Kedre counts in tens. It shares the numbers two, three, five and seven with Norsund (fovo, trimi, tammo, sevi).
Court Kedre is the speech of Keras, the decrees and the Church of Light.
Camp Kedre, the speech of the legions and traders in Thiolden, kept an old final -u (kividu, imperaru, denaru). Most Norsund loans were heard in camp Kedre.
The learned style of the Imperial Academy of Alchemy is full of participle nouns and passives.
Kedre arrived in Thiolden with Rechtar Vaire's conquest (37 to 51 a.v.e.) and Doir Vaire's rule over the Vilnayan towns.

Norsund borrowed Kedre words for walls, canals, markets, squares, towers and gates (mur, rie, merk, kamp, tur, port) and the subordinator ke, and later learned words such as alkimia, medikina and kupola.
Kedre borrowed runa from Norsund to name the rune magic of Thiolden; native Kedre runo only means "secret". Rundir Voidet's explosives were krepito runa, "rune powder".
Keras means "the Crowned" and Keria "the crown-land", the Empire. Rechtar means "ruler".
A Kedre name is a given name followed by a house name (Rechtar Vaire, Rundir Voidet).
The Emperor is keraro "crown-bearer" at court and imperaru "commander" among soldiers. The head of the Church of Light is the primaro, and Doir Vaire ruled Thiolden as reiato, "regent".
The Kedre names Exaire ("domain of the springs") and Arbaire ("domain of the trees") replaced the real-world names Exeter and Arbury in the lore records.

The surviving Kedre texts are the decree of year zero, the blessing of the Vaire bloodline, Rechtar's siege order at Marheim, a page of Rundir Voidet's notes, a hymn to Luxis, and Doir Vaire's proclamation to the Vilnayan towns.

facts: Most languages of Thiolden and the Vairean Empire descend from Proto-Valian, the deep ancestor language of the continent of Valia.
Norsund is the common tongue of Thiolden.
Kedre is the language of the Vairean Empire.
Proto-Valian split into Proto-Norsund, spoken on the island of Farheim, and the ancestor of Kedre, spoken in the north-west of Valia.
Proto-Norsund became Old Norsund, the language of the settlers who reached Thiolden around 450 b.v.e.
Old Norsund became Norsund around 100 a.v.e.

Norsund has several dialects. Starisund is the speech of Auristar; common Norsund is spoken in the Vilnayan towns; the Kullmyr, the Nurmyr and Farheim have their own varieties; the Thieves Guild of Auristar uses a backslang cant.
The sound changes and cognate sets that connect these languages are recorded in records/languages/norsund/grammar/13-history.yaml.

context: These languages are scoped but not yet built. Names from them keep their own spelling in Norsund texts.
Any apostrophe in a name stands for a real sound, as records/languages/norsund/grammar/02-orthography.yaml requires. Each entry says which.
facts: Dwarvish of Karhak'Modan: the tongue of the dwarves who hold the Pass of Kharak. Its apostrophe marks a glottal stop between the two elements of a compound name: Karhak'Modan is said [karhakʔmodan]. kh is a rasping [x], as in Scottish loch.
The Ik'nal'tar tongue: spoken by the people of Ik'nal'tar. Its apostrophe marks a glottal stop that closes a syllable: Ik'nal'tar is said [ikʔnalʔtar].

Ath'alan Elvish: the language of the elves descended from Ath'alan, the lineage of Othil, Lore Keeper of the Seven Lights. Its apostrophe marks a glottal stop between two syllables that would otherwise run together: Ath'alan is said [aθʔalan]. Elvish personal names such as Othil and Elenidas use no apostrophe.
Merfolk: the tongue of the Merfolk, which has its own runes, separate from the Old Norsund runes (records/user-submitted-stories/marv.yaml). No apostrophes are attested.

Vulkin and Nightvul: the speech of the Vulkin. The apostrophe joins a clan name to a given name and is said as a short glottal catch: Thor'Vale is [θorʔvale], 'Vale of clan Thor'. In Norsund company the given name alone is used (Vale).
Dragonkin: the speech of the Firewing Dragonkin and their kin (Gadrull). It is known for long rolled r and l sounds. No apostrophes are attested.
Ulfkin is the Norsund name for the wolf-folk formerly recorded as Worgenkin (Haakon's people). The word worgen belongs to another franchise.

context: Version 1.0.0 of the language, approved by the lore lead on 2026-11-19. Language files live beside this record in grammar/, dictionary/ and texts/.
Human-readable documentation is in docs/languages/norsund/. Tools for translating, writing and checking Norsund are in tools/.
facts: Norsund means "north-tongue" (nor "north" + sund "tongue, voice, song").
Norsund is the most common language of Thiolden and the second language of most of its races.
Thiolden means "land of the brave" in Norsund (thiol "brave" + den "land").
Norsund descends from Old Norsund, the language of the adventurers who settled Thiolden from the island of Farheim around 450 b.v.e.
Old Norsund descends from Proto-Norsund, spoken on Farheim, which descends from Proto-Valian, the deep ancestor of Valia's languages.
Kedre, the language of the Vairean Empire, is a distant cousin of Norsund; Lysmar and Luxis are the same word in the two branches.
The imperial conquest of Thiolden (37 to 51 a.v.e.) left a layer of Kedre words in Norsund for walls, canals, markets, towers and gates, much as the Norman conquest left French words in English.
Old Norsund is still used for oaths, law, temple liturgy and rune-craft.
Starisund ("star-tongue") is the speech of Auristar. It treats stars as living beings, calls seven stev, and softens th to s.
Common Norsund is spoken in the Vilnayan towns and across Thiolden.
The Kullmyr say i for y (Firen for Fyren); the Nurmyr drop initial h; Farheim keeps the oldest forms.
The Thieves Guild of Auristar uses a backslang cant.
Norsund is written in runes (runar) for everyday use across Thiolden, and in Lysrit ("light-writing") for sacred and civic texts in Auristar.
Rune magic happens only when runes are charged with aether, which makes them glow. Auristar forbids rune magic but not rune writing, so runes in Auristar never glow.
In English-language lore, Norsund is written in a plain ASCII romanization with no accents or apostrophes.
The glyph shapes of both scripts are final for version 1.0, with production treatments for stone, glass, UI, wood, slate and embroidery.
Reference recordings of every canon name, the phrasebook and the sample texts are in assets/audio/norsund, generated from the language's IPA.
Speakers mark how they know what they say with sa ("I saw it"), sund ("so it is sung") or stari ("so the stars say").
Court testimony in Auristar must carry sa, or it counts as hearsay.
Tavern cooks are called fyr ("fire").
Norsund pronouns mark living versus non-living, not sex or gender.
Auristar is pronounced OW-ree-star; au is always as in "cow".
Myr and Heid are the old Wandering-House names of Ur and Nett, not four separate gods.
Stars are grammatically animate in Starisund and inanimate elsewhere.
Runes are allowed in Auristar as plain, non-glowing writing; only rune magic is forbidden.
aur "silver-bright" is a native Norsund word, so Auristar is a fully native name.

facts: Old Norsund is the language of the adventurers who settled Thiolden from the island of Farheim around 450 b.v.e.
Old Norsund was the everyday language of Marheim and the first Vilnayan villages.
Old Norsund gave way to Norsund around 100 a.v.e., about the time the First Ring of the Kjoldmur was finished.
Vilkyr ("free sword") is an Old Norsund word that Norsund kept unchanged.
Old Norsund descends from Proto-Norsund, spoken on Farheim, and ultimately from Proto-Valian.
The name Thiolden comes from the Old Norsund phrase den thiolini, "land of the brave ones", spoken by the settlers' leader at the landfall.
Old Norsund has the same sounds as Norsund, plus an initial hw (hwander), a g between vowels (negi), the diphthong ey, and full vowels in endings.
Old Norsund was written in runes on wood, bone and slate. Carvers did not mark long vowels or double consonants, so a carving can be read more than one way.
Scholars cite Old Norsund with þ, ð and acute accents for long vowels (þjol, veða, tír); lore writers use the plain spelling (thiol, vetha, tiir).
Nouns have four cases (nominative, accusative, genitive, dative). Animate nouns mark the object with -a, and every preposition takes the dative.
The word for "the" was hin, a separate word placed after the noun; Norsund fused it into the suffix -in.
Adjectives agree with their noun in case and number.
Verbs agree with singular and plural subjects (kjoldur "guards", kjoldum "they guard"), in the present and the past.
Wishes, blessings and curses use the optative ending -i; the future uses hala "to owe" with an infinitive.
Main clauses put the verb second and subordinate clauses put it last; ne always comes directly before the verb.
Old Norsund has no evidential particles. Oaths name the gods as witnesses instead.
Ten is dovthamm, "two hands", and markets counted in the long hundred (langhaun, 120).
A person is named by given name and parent-name in -ung ("child of"); a famous person adds a byname followed by hin, as in Tyr thiol hin, "Tyr the brave".
A noble house is "the children of" its founder, written with -ungin.
Memorial stones follow a fixed formula and end with a ban on charging their runes, because rune magic near the dead raises them.
Vilkyr oaths are sworn in Old Norsund.
The laws carved on the Kjoldmur are written in Old Norsund, and the laws of the Marheim moot were recited in it.
The oldest temple invocations of Auristar are in Old Norsund and use the old god-names Myr and Heid.
Sagas such as the Saga of the Wanderers are recited in Old Norsund by the Sundwanderen.
Rune-craft formulas and incantations are composed in Old Norsund. Charging runes makes them glow; this is rune magic, and it is forbidden in Auristar.
Farheim island speech keeps some Old Norsund forms in songs.
Unstressed i and u in final syllables became e, so -in and -ur turned into -en and -er (Vilkyrin to Vilkyren, kjoldur to kjolder).
g between vowels became j and merged into the diphthong ei (negi to nay); initial hw became w (hwander to wander); long vowels shortened outside the first syllable (iliin to ilin).
The cases and number agreement fell away, the article fused onto the noun, and the Kedre loan ke replaced the relative particle ys.

facts.The evidentials grew from Old Norsund wo: sa is the past of saja "see", sund is "song", and stari is "of the stars".

facts: The Old Norsund law that a witness who did not see may not swear is the origin of Auristar's rule that testimony needs the evidential sa.

facts: Norsund is written in two native scripts, the runes (runar) and Lysrit ("light-writing"). In English-language lore it uses a plain ASCII romanization.
The runes are the everyday script of Thiolden, inherited from the Old Norsund settlers of Farheim. Rune slates, Vilnayan woodwork, boundary stones and merchants' tallies use them.
Runes are ordinary writing. They become rune magic only when a carver charges them with aether, and a charged rune glows.
Auristar forbids rune magic, not rune writing. Runes are seen everywhere in Auristar, but they never glow there.
The rune row (runrad) has 24 staves. kj and gj are written as k and g with a palatal dot, so 26 sounds are covered.
Consonant runes carry their branches on the right of the stave and vowel runes on the left, so rune-readers say consonants "look forward" and vowels "look back".
Each rune is named after a Norsund word that begins with its sound, such as kyr "blade" for k and lys "light" for l. The ng rune is named ung "offspring" because no word begins with ng.
Runes come in two forms. Long-branch runes are cut in stone; short-twig runes are a faster form for wood and everyday notes.
The Kullmyr treat runes as living beings and call them runen; everyone else says runar.
Merfolk runes are a separate tradition.
Lysrit is Auristar's sacred and civic script, used on temples, the Kjoldmur, the decrees of the Seven Lights, and anything holy.
Scholars of the Starlight Library designed it after the First Ring of the Kjoldmur was completed (c. 99-124 a.v.e.), which is why it is systematic rather than evolved.
Every Lysrit letter is drawn on the grid of Auristar's seven-pointed emblem, with the top point up and a centre.
Consonants are straight strokes between the seven points; sounds made in the same part of the mouth share a base bar.
Vowels are stars placed on a point of the grid, as on a vowel chart. A lit centre marks a voiced sound.
One consonant and the vowel stars that follow it share one cell, so every word looks like a small constellation.
Lysrit numbers trace the rim of the heptagon. Seven is the closed heptagon, the "full count".
A violet seven-pointed star before a word marks a holy name.
In Auristar, lit windows and crystal studs can spell Lysrit words across a tower face at night.
The glyph shapes of Lysrit and the runes are final for version 1.0.

Each medium has a treatment: carved white stone with crystal inlay, stained-glass domes, techwear and game UI, wood and slate runes, and embroidery. Each sets stroke weights, terminals, minimum sizes, colours and glow rules, in docs/languages/norsund/writing-systems.md (Production art direction).
The reference art sheets are generated by tools/fonts/art_sheets.mjs into docs/languages/norsund/img/art-*.svg.
Only Lysrit stars may shine; a glowing rune is always rune magic.
